newsitem.title: UK: IRA claims Lisburn bomb, demands talks.
newsitem.headline: IRA claims Lisburn bomb, demands talks.

text.p: The Irish Republican Army (IRA) claimed responsibility for bombing Britain's Northern Ireland army headquarters on Monday and demanded that Britain invite its Sinn Fein political wing to peace talks.

"The resolution of the conflict demands an inclusive negotiated settlement. This is not possible unless and until the British Government faces up to its responsibilities," the IRA said in a statement to Irish state broadcaster RTE.
It was the first time the IRA, which fights to end British rule of Northern Ireland, had attacked a target in Northern Ireland since it ended a 17-month ceasefire in February.
Sinn Fein, which shares the IRA's goal of reuniting the two Irelands, is barred from the peace talks because of the IRA's decision to end its truce.
The attack was viewed by security forces and the British government as the most serious development in Northern Ireland since Britain and Ireland embarked on a peace initiative in December 1993.

The IRA accused Britain of "squandering" the opportunity presented by its unprecedented 17-month ceasefire by insisting that the guerrillas prove willing to disarm to earn Sinn Fein a seat with other parties at Belfast peace talks.
"The British Government responded by squandering that historic opportunity in a vain attempt to defeat the IRA," the statement said.
Prime Minister John Major, speaking to reporters at the annual conference of his Conservative party, described the IRA claim of responsibility as "sickening".
The claim brought back echoes of the worst days of Northern Ireland's 27-year political and sectarian troubles when near-daily violence killed 3,200 and turned the province into a British fortress.

It also increased fears among ordinary Catholics of revenge attacks by Protestant Loyalist gunmen who have stuck by their own two-year-old ceasefire to earn their political spokesmen a place at Belfast peace talks.
The IRA denied media speculation that its units had targetted Northern Ireland to provoke Loyalist retaliation and wreck the Belfast peace talks altogether.
It said its target was army personnel at the Lisburn base "barracks and we regret any injuries caused to civilians.
The twin car bombs injured a total of 31 people, 20 of them soldiers. Twelve were still in hospital on Tuesday, three of them seriously wounded police said.
Spokesmen for the Loyalists' political wings appealed all day to their military allies not to resort to revenge attacks of the sort which killed 900 Catholics before the truce was called.
The Loyalists' umbrella organisation, the Combined Loyalist Military Command, was reported by Northern Ireland media to have met on Tuesday to study its next step but made no statement.
Army chiefs began an immediate review of security at their Lisburn headquarters to determine how anyone could get past a security cordon with explosives concealed in their vehicles.
The IRA has said it will not discuss any arms handover until there is an agreed political settlement between Irish nationalists and the 60 percent pro-British Protestant majority.

There was no sign that either Britain or Ireland would abandon their insistence on an end to IRA violence as the key to Sinn Fein's entry into the talks, nor that they might abandon the negotiations, which have faltered since opening in June.
"No consideration has been given to postponing the talks," Irish Prime Minister John Bruton told the Irish Parliament.
